rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A heated liquid's true growth is its **absolute (real) expansion** $\Delta V_r = \gamma_r V_0 \Delta T$, but a vessel observer sees only the **apparent expansion** $\Delta V_a = \gamma_a V_0 \Delta T$, because the vessel's cavity expands too: $\gamma_r = \gamma_a + \gamma_g$ (γ_g = 3α of the vessel material). Density falls as $\rho_T = \rho_0/(1+\gamma_r\Delta T)$.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - γ_r = γ_a + γ_g - ρ_T = ρ₀/(1 + γ_rΔT) - Water: max density at 4 °C

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Real vs apparent:** you see the apparent; the real includes the vessel's own expansion: γ_r = γ_a + γ_g.  ·  **Water's anomaly is 0–4 °C only** — above 4 °C water behaves normally.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Liquids Take the Shape of the Question A heated liquid expands — but observed through a container, part of the expansion is swallowed by the expanding glass. Physics separates the **apparent** expansion (what you see) from the **absolute** expansion (what really happens): their difference is the container's expansion.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Real (absolute) and apparent expansion When a liquid in a vessel of volume $V_0$ is heated by ΔT: - **Absolute (real) expansion:** the true volume increase of the liquid: $\Delta V_{real} = \gamma_r V_0 \Delta T$, with γ_r the **coefficient of absolute (real) cubical expansion**.…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 47:** γ_r and γ_a are cubical coefficients; the vessel's γ_g = 3α_glass. - **To Topic 49:** Dulong–Petit measures γ_r using the apparent expansion in two different vessels. - **To density bottle / hydrometer:** liquid expansion instruments.
